sections.body_en:
There is a Torah mitzva not to eat sheratzim (creeping and swarming creatures), as it is stated (Vayikra 11:43-44): "You shall not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, nor shall you make yourselves unclean with them, that you should be defiled by them. For I am the Lord your God; sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy; and you shall not defile yourselves with any manner of swarming thing that moves upon the earth." There are three kinds of sheratzim: water sheratzim, land sheratzim and flying sheratzim, and regarding each one of them the Torah added a separate command.

Water sheratzim, as it is stated (ibid. 10-11): "And all that do not have fins and scales in the seas and in the rivers, of all that swarm in the waters and of all the living creatures that are in the waters, they are a detestable thing to you. And they shall be a detestable thing to you; you shall not eat of their flesh, and their carcasses you shall hold in detestation." Included among water sheratzim are crabs, leeches, worms that live in water, and even seals (literally "sea dogs"). But a creature that looks like a fish and swims in the water like a fish, if it does not have fins and scales, is forbidden as a non-kosher fish and not as a water sheretz (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 2:12).

Land sheratzim, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:41-44): "And every swarming thing that swarms upon the earth is a detestable thing; it shall not be eaten. Whatever goes upon its belly, and whatever goes upon all fours, or whatever has many feet, of all swarming things that swarm upon the earth, you shall not eat them, for they are a detestable thing… and you shall not defile yourselves with any manner of swarming thing that moves upon the earth." Included among land sheratzim are worms, spiders, ants, beetles, lizards, snakes, scorpions and mice. But a creature that looks like a wild or domestic animal, if it lacks the signs of a kosher animal, is forbidden as a non-kosher animal and not as a land sheretz.

Flying sheratzim, as it is stated (Devarim 14:19): "And every winged swarming thing is unclean to you; they shall not be eaten." Included among them are flies, mosquitoes, gnats, bees, wasps, non-kosher locusts and the like. But a creature that looks like a bird and flies like a bird, if it is not one of the kosher birds, is forbidden as a non-kosher bird and not as a flying sheretz.

From the fact that the Torah repeated the prohibitions of sheratzim many times and in different expressions, the Sages learned that the punishment of one who eats a water sheretz is four sets of lashes, a land sheretz – five sets of lashes, and a flying sheretz – six sets of lashes (Makkot 16b). In this the prohibition of sheratzim is more severe than other food prohibitions, for one who eats a non-kosher fish, or a non-kosher animal such as a pig, or a non-kosher bird such as a raven, is liable to one set of thirty-nine lashes, whereas one who eats a sheretz is liable to several sets. In addition, as a rule, only one who eats the measure of a kezayit is liable to the punishment set by the Torah. However, with a sheretz there is a special stringency: since it is a whole creature, anyone who eats even a small sheretz is liable to the punishment set by the Torah (Mishna Makkot 13a; Shevu'ot 21b).1

notes_en.en: "Lashes" means a set of thirty-nine lashes. In practice this punishment was intended mainly as a deterrent, since it is carried out only when the sin was committed deliberately, before witnesses and after a warning; but we learn from it about the severity of the sin. One who eats a whole sheretz, even a small one, is liable to lashes. If it was crushed, he is liable only if he ate a kezayit, for since it is not a whole creature (beria), its law is like that of other forbidden foods. One who touches one of the sheratzim does not become impure; however, there are eight sheratzim that after their death impart impurity to whoever touches them: the ḥoled, the akhbar, the tzav, the anaka, the ko'aḥ, the leta'a, the ḥomet and the tinshemet (Vayikra 11:29-30). Since with regard to impurity a lentil's measure of their flesh imparts impurity, so too the law regarding eating: even if one ate a lentil's measure of their flesh, he is liable to lashes (Me'ila 16b). Many sheratzim are small and tiny, but it seems straightforward that the Torah forbade a sheretz whose taste or swallowing can be sensed, whereas a tiny sheretz whose taste and swallowing are not felt carries no Torah prohibition (as explained below, n. 14).

sections.title_en: The Mitzva to Keep Away from What Is Disgusting
sections.body_en:
We learned another mitzva from the prohibition of sheratzim: it is forbidden for a person to do disgusting and repulsive things, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:43-44): "You shall not make yourselves detestable." That is, by the prohibition of eating sheratzim the Torah intended to keep us away from anything that is considered repulsive in people's eyes. Therefore, it is forbidden to eat repulsive foods, or to eat in a manner that arouses a feeling of disgust (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 17:29-30; SA 116:6; Peninei Halakha: Berakhot 13:5-6, 13).2

All forbidden foods are called "impure" (teme'im), and eating them defiles the soul and blocks it from absorbing matters of holiness, for tum'a (impurity) is related to timtum (obtuseness) (Yoma 39a). The impurity in the prohibition of sheratzim is especially severe, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:43-45): "You shall not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, nor shall you make yourselves unclean with them, that you should be defiled by them. For I am the Lord your God; sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy; and you shall not defile yourselves with any manner of swarming thing that moves upon the earth. For I am the Lord who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God; you shall therefore be holy, for I am holy." The Sages said (Bava Metzia 61b): "The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Had I brought Israel up out of Egypt only for this matter, that they do not defile themselves with sheratzim – it would have been enough for Me." For eating sheratzim is extremely repulsive, since they grow in filthy places and their swarming disgusts the soul, and through refraining from eating them God brought us up out of the impurity of Egypt. That is, the impurity that leads a person to give up his values for the sake of satisfying his bodily desires, to the point that, in order to amass wealth and pleasures, people turned free men into slaves, and in order to satisfy their bodily desires they violated the covenant of faithfulness between a man and his wife through every kind of adultery (based on Maharal; Peninei Halakha: Pesaḥ 1:3-4).

One may explain that among sheratzim no distinctive character trait is evident; rather, all their vitality and diligence are focused on the most material goal: obtaining food and reproducing. For this purpose they soil themselves in all the disgusting things in the world, and wherever there is rot and death, there they swarm, and they even eat the human corpse. Admittedly, this vitality contains a basic existential need, which also has an important place in the world. But Israel, who are holy and must elevate and uplift reality from the impurity of Egypt and reveal the Divine value in everything, were commanded not to eat sheratzim, which express repulsive materiality.3

notes_en.en: From the Gemara (Shabbat 90b) it is clear that one who eats a live kosher locust transgresses "bal teshaktzu" ("you shall not make yourselves detestable"), since it is a repulsive thing (above 17:8). According to the Yere'im, Semak, Ramah and Mor U-ketzi'a, this prohibition is from the Torah, and likewise all repulsive things are forbidden by Torah law, except that one does not receive lashes for them (because it is a "lav she-bikhlalot," a general prohibition), and the Sages instituted that one be given disciplinary lashes (makat mardut). Many wrote that the prohibition is rabbinic, among them: Ritva, Meiri, Rashbatz, Levush, Pri Ḥadash 116:11; Magen Avraham 92:2; MB 7.

The Or Ha-ḥayim wrote (Vayikra 11:43) that one who eats sheratzim "deliberately – his soul becomes a detestable thing; and unintentionally – his soul becomes defiled and dulled." However, if he checked as required, or ate under duress because he was not required to check, he did not transgress the prohibition, and eating the sheretz does not dull his soul (Rav Pe'alim vol. 4, Sod Yesharim 6).

sections.title_en: The Prohibition Applies to Sheratzim That Can Swarm
sections.body_en:
The forbidden water sheratzim are sheratzim that grew in seas, rivers and springs, that is, in expanses in which they are able to swarm – meaning, to move to additional places of growth and multiply in enormous numbers by obtaining food and producing offspring for generations. But sheratzim that grew in standing water found in pits and caves, as long as the sheratzim have not left it, are considered part of the water and are not forbidden, and one may drink from it even though the sheratzim are in it. But if the water is taken from there in a vessel, since the sheratzim in it have already left their place of growth, they become forbidden, and it is forbidden to drink the water without straining it. Sheratzim that grew within water or other liquids in a vessel, even if the water they are in is poured from vessel to vessel, remain permitted, because all vessels are considered their place of growth. Only from the moment they leave the water to fly in the air or to crawl on the outside wall of the vessel does the prohibition take effect on them (SA and Rema 84:1, 3).

Similarly, the forbidden land sheratzim and flying sheratzim are the sheratzim that grow on the ground and on anything resting on the ground, as it is stated (Vayikra 11:41): "And every swarming thing that swarms upon the earth is a detestable thing; it shall not be eaten." But sheratzim that developed inside detached fruit, or inside meat, fish or cheese, as long as they crawl inside them and have not gone out, are not forbidden, because they are not in a place where they can swarm, that is, multiply in enormous numbers by obtaining new food and producing offspring for generations. Therefore they are still subordinate to the fruit or food in which they develop and are considered part of it. From the moment they go out, they become forbidden, since they have begun to swarm, that is, to multiply, upon the earth (SA 84:4).4

notes_en.en:
It was commonly thought that the worms that developed in fruit were generated from the rotting of the fruit. Today it is clear that they came from eggs laid there by sheratzim. But in practice the law does not change, since the principle is that a worm that formed inside a fruit, as long as it has not swarmed on the ground, is permitted.
All agree that sheratzim that developed in detached fruit are permitted, and some are lenient even regarding worms that swarmed in the fruit while it was still attached to the tree (Rashi, Rabbenu Tam, Rabbenu Netanel, Or Zaru'a, Ra'avya and Riva, based on Ḥullin 67b). However, according to most Rishonim, the halakha follows Shmuel (Ḥullin 58a) that as long as the fruits are attached to the tree, the worms in them are considered as swarming on the ground and are forbidden by Torah law; and so wrote the She'iltot, Behag, Rif, Rambam (2:15), Ran, Rashba, Rosh, Terumah, Riaz and Nimukei Yosef. And so it was ruled in the Tur and SA 84:6. According to many, the approach of the lenient authorities is combined to form a safek sefeika (double doubt) (Ginat Veradim, Shulḥan Gavo'ah, Ben Avraham, Ziv'ḥei Tzedek 84:42; Halikhot Olam vol. 6 p. 262; Tefilla Le-Moshe 6:37; they disagree with SA 84:7, who holds that their approach is not combined to form a safek sefeika). Regarding a larva, the poskim disagreed (below, n. 20).
The Sages were in doubt about the law of a worm that did not fully leave the fruit but only partially emerged, or that crawled inside a cavity formed in the fruit or on its surface, or that passed from fruit to fruit, or that fell from the fruit and died while in the air (Ḥullin 67b). The Rishonim wrote that this is a doubt regarding a Torah law, and the ruling is to be stringent (SA 84:4). If it died and afterward came out: according to Rashi, Tosafot, Rosh, the unattributed opinion in SA 84:4, Shakh and Pleti, it is permitted; and according to Rif, Rambam, Knesset Ha-gedola, Pri To'ar and Shulḥan Gavo'ah, it is forbidden. A detached fruit that has a hole with a worm in it: according to Rashba and SA 84:4, it is permitted, for we are not concerned that it emerged and returned; and according to Terumat Ha-deshen, Mordekhai and Rema, it is forbidden, lest it emerged and returned.
A water sheretz that grew inside a pit or a vessel and rose out of the water and crawled on the wall of the pit or vessel or on its rim is still considered as not having left its place of growth and is not forbidden. But if it moved to the outer wall of the pit or vessel, it becomes forbidden by Torah law. And even if it returns to the water, it remains forbidden. However, as long as it is inside the water in which it grew, we are not concerned that it emerged and returned, except with flying or large sheratzim, where there is a reasonable concern that they emerged and returned to the pit (Pri Megadim 84, Siftei Da'at 10).
Water drawn in a vessel from the pit: the sheratzim in it become forbidden, lest they emerged onto the inner wall of the vessel, which is no longer considered their place of growth (Rosh, Rema 84:1, Baḥ and Shakh. Some say the concern is lest they stick to the outer wall of the vessel and afterward enter the water – Taz 5). But sheratzim that grew in water inside a vessel, even if the water was poured into another vessel, are not forbidden, for all vessels are considered their place of growth (Beit Yosef and Rema 84:3).

sections.title_en: A Whole Creature (Beria) Is Not Nullified
sections.body_en:
Continuing the Torah's special stringency, which established that one who eats a sheretz, even a small one, is liable to lashes (above, 1), the Sages established that if a sheretz becomes mixed into food, as long as it is whole, since it has the importance of a beria (a complete creature), it is not nullified. According to several Rishonim (Rash, Or Zaru'a and Rashba), although a beria is not nullified in sixty, in close to a thousand (960) it is nullified. Several of the great Aḥaronim wrote that in a pressing situation one may rely on their opinion. However, as a rule it was ruled that a beria is not nullified even in a thousand. Therefore, if people saw a fly enter a huge pot full of cooked food and did not manage to find it and remove it, the entire dish is forbidden to eat. However, if the dish contains clear broth, one may strain it through a strainer that a fly cannot pass through, and the strained broth is permitted. Likewise, if the dish contains pieces of meat or potatoes, they can be permitted by rinsing, which will remove the fly if it was stuck to them. But the thick mixture and the pieces that are hard to clean are forbidden (SA 100:2-3). Similarly, if a small sheretz became mixed into grains of wheat, as long as it has not been found, the mixture is forbidden, because it is not nullified even in a thousand.

If part of the sheretz was cut off, even a small part such as a leg, or it was crushed until its form changed, as commonly happens during cooking, it does not have the importance of a beria and is nullified in sixty (SA 100:1). According to many, even a tiny sheretz found in food, although it is whole, does not have the importance of a beria and is nullified in sixty (Mishkenot Ya'akov YD 36; Pitḥei Teshuva 100:1; Ḥokhmat Shlomo 84:1; Yad Yehuda, and others; below, n. 12).5

notes_en.en:
In the Ran (on the Rif, 36b) an opinion is cited, based on the Yerushalmi (Terumot 10:5), that a beria is nullified in a thousand (and it is cited in Beit Yosef 100:4). According to Rash, Or Zaru'a, Rashba and Kaftor Va-feraḥ, a beria is nullified in 960. According to most Rishonim, a beria is not nullified even in a thousand; this is the opinion of Tosafot, Ramban, Ra'ah, Rosh, Ritva, Ran and others, and so it was ruled in SA 100:1.
In Nazir 51b a doubt is raised and left unresolved: whether one who eats a sheretz from which a limb that it can live without was cut off is liable to lashes. The Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 2:22) that he does not receive lashes. The Ramban added that it has also lost the status of a beria and is nullified in sixty. And so wrote the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim, among them Rashba, Rosh, Ran and Ritva. And so wrote SA 100:6: "But if they were cut or crushed until their form was lost, they are nullified, for they are no longer considered important." The implication is that even if it was squashed until its form changed, it has lost the status of a beria. This is also implied by the Rashba (Torat Ha-bayit, Bayit 3, end of Sha'ar 3), who holds that after cooking there is a doubt whether perhaps the beria dissolved and was nullified. And so wrote many poskim, among them Pri Megadim (Siftei Da'at 100:6), Nishmat Adam, Ḥazon Ish and others (and see Bi'ur Ha-Gra 101:17).
Sheratzim that have lost the status of a beria: if their taste is spoiled, they are nullified in a majority (Taz 96:13; Ḥokhmat Adam 38:27), and if their taste is not spoiled, they are nullified in sixty (Rema 84:9; Shakh 30).

sections.body_en:
The Torah forbade eating sheratzim, not fruits in which sheratzim might be hidden; and if a situation arises in which a person senses the taste of a sheretz while eating, he should spit out what is in his mouth. However, it emerges from the words of the Sages that when there is a reasonable chance that the fruits contain sheratzim, one may not eat the fruits without checking (Ḥullin 58a). The poskim explained that there are three situations in this:

a) Foods that usually contain sheratzim, such as foods that were kept in a filthy place, are considered presumed to contain sheratzim (muḥzakim be-sheratzim), and it is obligatory to check them. As long as they have not been checked or cleaned of the sheratzim, it is forbidden to eat them.

b) Foods that most of the time do not contain sheratzim, but a "common minority" (mi'ut ha-matzui) of which contain sheratzim, require checking; but after the fact, when there is no possibility of checking them, it is permitted to follow the majority and eat them.

c) Foods that usually do not contain sheratzim, even though they sometimes do contain sheratzim, may be eaten without checking. This is the situation of most of the foods, fruits and vegetables available to us, in which only an "uncommon minority" contain sheratzim. However, if signs of rot, webs or holes are seen in them, they rise to the level of being presumed to contain sheratzim, and it is obligatory to check them.

The overwhelming majority of the poskim did not define what a "common minority" is, nor did they determine the unit by which majority and minority are determined; thus they intended to leave the matter in the hands of each person, so that according to what he knows and understands, he will decide at what level of concern the food before him stands. And although several poskim tried to partially define the concept of "common minority," in practice they did not give a definition by which the status of all foods can be determined, since the frequency of sheratzim depends not only on the type of food but also on the conditions in which it was grown and stored. When the vegetable is grown and stored in conditions of heat and humidity, the sheratzim multiply, and in conditions of cold they decrease, to the point where they are unable to develop. Likewise, the longer the food is stored and the dirtier the place, the greater the chance that sheratzim will multiply in it. Thus, it is impossible to determine the obligation of checking according to the type of food or the season of the year. Therefore, we must say that the responsibility for determining the status of the food depends on a person's awareness: each person, according to who he is and in accordance with the levels we learned above, will determine whether the obligation to check applies to him. However, kashrut organizations must set clearer definitions, as will be explained in the note.6

A food known not to be presumed to contain sheratzim in which three sheratzim were found – all the food in that vessel or package becomes presumed to contain sheratzim, and it is forbidden to eat it without checking (SA 100:4; 84:9).7

notes_en.en:
The Rosh, Rashba and Ran learned from Ḥullin 58b that dates must be checked, since sheratzim are commonly found in them. The Rashba (Torat Ha-bayit Ha-arokh 3:3) and the Ran wrote that even when only a minority of the dates contain sheratzim, they should be checked, just as one must check the lungs for adhesions (sirkhot), which are commonly found in a minority of them. Likewise, the Rashba and Beit Yosef 84:8 learned from Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 2:15, that fruits that tend to become wormy even in only a "common minority" require checking. The Rashba wrote that if one transgressed and cooked the food without checking, and it can no longer be checked, the food is kosher, just as an animal whose lungs were lost before checking is kosher. And so it was ruled in SA 84:8-9; Shakh 29. All this is according to most poskim, who hold that by rabbinic law one must check in a situation of a "common minority"; but there are Rishonim who hold that there is no obligation to check foods in which a "common minority" contain sheratzim, since we follow the majority (Rashi, Rashbam, Tosafot Pesaḥim 115b, s.v. "kafa").
And some say that although as a rule one must check foods in which a "common minority" contain sheratzim, when this involves great difficulty there is no obligation to check in a case of a "common minority"; rather we rely on the majority and permit eating (Mishkenot Ya'akov YD 17; Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, third edition, 1:158).
What is a "common minority": As I wrote above, the overwhelming majority of the poskim did not deal with defining "common minority," so they intended that each person decide this according to his awareness. However, in recent generations we have become accustomed to measuring everything in numbers and percentages, and without this we find it difficult to settle our awareness, and the need arose to try to quantify the measure of a "common minority." This is especially true of kashrut organizations, which cannot determine their position in every case according to the personal assessment of the mashgiaḥ. Therefore they went back to examine the words of the poskim closely in order to find a numerical definition. In Responsa Rivash 191, he wrote that a "common minority" is "close to half and occurring regularly." And so wrote Beit Efrayim YD 6. My teacher and master Rav Yisraeli (Ha-Torah Ve-ha-aretz vol. 3 p. 151), Rav Mazuz and Mishneh Halakhot 7:99 leaned toward his view. It seems that the Rivash meant between about 25% and 49%. And one should not say that less than 40% is already not "close to half," for they did not require this to be checked precisely, and it is difficult for a person to distinguish in his assessment between 40% and 30%. On the other hand, it is clear that he did not mean less than 25%, since that is not considered "close to half." Another opinion is that of Mishkenot Ya'akov YD 17, who brought a source showing that already from 10% it is a "common minority," that is, "frequently found." And many customarily rule like him, as cited in Darkhei Teshuva 39:3; Yeshu'at Moshe vol. 3, 62:3; Minḥat Shlomo vol. 2, 61:1; Ekhol Be-simḥa p. 212.
Still, the matter remains difficult, since the question depends on the size of the unit by which majority and minority are determined. The larger the unit of measurement, the greater the chances that a sheretz will be found in it, and consequently more foods will require checking. If, for example, the unit of measurement were a large warehouse, presumably at least one sheretz would be found in all foods, and then all foods would require checking. Conversely, if the unit of measurement is a gram, no food would be presumed to contain sheratzim. In practice there are four possibilities, and each is correct from a different angle: a) A meal: from the angle of the one preparing the meal, it makes no difference whether he sifted flour for two diners or for ten, since each time he sifts flour, the flour he sifted is considered in his awareness as one unit (and I leaned toward this below in halakha 16 regarding flour). b) A portion: from the angle of the one eating, a portion is the unit present in his awareness (so wrote Rav Ze'ev Weitman and Rav Yoel Friedman). c) A food item: if we focus our awareness on the food, the unit is as the food appears before us, a fruit or a vegetable, whether large or small (see Ḥatam Sofer 2:77). And it seems that with packaged foods such as flour and legumes, it is the package as it is before us, a kilo or half a kilo. d) One bite: if we focus our awareness on the halakhic angle, we relate to each bite as a unit in itself, since it is the act of eating, and consequently the units should be determined by it. (See SA 109:1, that from the perspective of halakhic awareness each bite is considered a unit in itself.) Apparently, since each of the possibilities is more suited to a certain type of food or occasion, the poskim did not define this halakha; rather it must be determined according to the impression that the presence of sheratzim in each food leaves on one's awareness (my teacher and master Rav Yisraeli wrote similarly in Ha-Torah Ve-ha-aretz vol. 3 p. 151). It further seems that the larger the sheretz, the more space it occupies in one's awareness, and one should be concerned about it even at a lower frequency and with larger units of measurement.
Still the problem has not been solved: what does one do when we are in doubt as to which awareness determines the measure of a "common minority," and especially, how should kashrut organizations act when they serve different people with different awarenesses? In practice, it seems that the average awareness is that the unit is a person's average portion, which is also the most constant and the most convenient for calculation, since it does not depend on the size of the family or of the fruit or the package. However, in case of need, since the basis of the obligation to check is rabbinic, one may be lenient and measure by the bite. All the more so when dealing with tiny sheratzim, where one should calculate by the bite (as explained below in halakha 7, nn. 13, 15).
However, it seems that when it is known regarding a food that in most cases large sheratzim are found in it, such that their taste can be sensed while eating, it is forbidden by Torah law to eat it without checking, since we follow the majority. However, there is still a doubt as to how the majority is determined, by bites or by meals, and since it is a doubt regarding a Torah law, one must be stringent. Some rabbis of our time wrote that in a situation of a majority, even when the taste of the sheretz cannot be sensed, the obligation to check is by Torah law (Rav Yehuda Amiḥai in Emunat Itekha 11 p. 21; Rav Yigal Hadaya, ibid. 35 p. 30; Rav Revaḥ in Tola'at Shani 7:2). However, as we learned, the course of the talmudic discussion is not so, and it seems that their words have no well-founded source.

However, when it is known that the three sheratzim were not mixed into the food from the start but came to it from outside, and it is reasonable that they are the only ones, the food is kosher. And if it is reasonable that just as three sheratzim reached the food, so more reached it, the food is forbidden without checking (see Taz 84:17).
A fruit in which a "common minority" contain sheratzim – checking a sample of it does not help (Responsa Rashba 1:274). But it seems that when there is a doubt about this, one may check a sample of it.
The Rashba wrote (Torat Ha-bayit, Bayit 3, end of Sha'ar 3) that if one transgressed and cooked a food that needed to be checked, one may be lenient because it is a safek sefeika: first, perhaps there was no sheretz there; second, and if there was, perhaps it dissolved and was nullified. End quote. Some say that the reasoning of safek sefeika applies even to food presumed to contain sheratzim, for since it does not always contain sheratzim, there is a safek sefeika to be lenient (Peraḥ Shoshan; Torat Netanel 38; Teshuva Me-ahava YD 330, and others). According to most poskim, safek sefeika to be lenient was stated only regarding a common minority, but a food that in most cases contains sheratzim is considered presumed to be forbidden and is not regarded as a doubt (Issur Ve-heter He-arokh, Maharam of Lublin, Shakh 29, Pri Megadim Siftei Da'at 32, Arukh Ha-shulḥan 70-72). If vegetables remain from the same bunch, one should check their condition: if three sheratzim are found in them, there is a presumption that the vegetables mixed into the dish also contain sheratzim, and the dish is forbidden; and if three sheratzim are not found in them, the dish is kosher.

sections.body_en:
It is agreed that there is no need to check for tiny sheratzim that the human eye cannot see, since the Torah commanded a person according to his natural ability to see. The problem is that it is hard to determine the size of the sheretz one must look for, because people's eyesight differs from one person to another, and it also depends on the color of the sheretz and on the background on which it is found. A person with good eyesight can see, against a white background, large microbes whose size is five hundredths of a millimeter; but when the color of the sheretz is similar to the background on which it is found, even if it is ten times larger, he will not manage to see it, and only experts in this may perhaps manage to see it. Even a sheretz two millimeters in size is not always found by people with good eyesight, but when it is pointed out to them, they will see it. That is, seeing a sheretz depends on several factors: a) its size; b) the quality of the eyesight; c) the color of the sheretz and its background; d) familiarity with the sheratzim; e) the state of the sheretz – if it is crawling, it is easier to see.8

Some are stringent and hold that when dealing with a vegetable or fruit known to be presumed to contain sheratzim, one must check for every sheretz that can be seen under optimal conditions. When it is difficult to check it under ordinary conditions, one must use experts in the matter or a light table and the like, and only after it has been clarified with certainty that it contains no sheretz at all is it permitted to eat it. And when it cannot be checked properly, it is forbidden to eat it. Therefore the stringent authorities ruled not to eat vegetables such as corn on the cob and cauliflower, which cannot be checked properly, and they composed series of books defining the status of each and every species, the sheratzim commonly found in it, and the obligation to check it (Rav Vaye and Rav Revaḥ).9

On the other hand, some permit and hold that the halakha is determined according to what people actually see, and there is no prohibition to eat a fruit or vegetable containing tiny sheratzim that people with good eyesight do not see with ordinary sight. And since this was the practice of the Jewish people for many generations, it is not right to be stringent in this, so as not to cast aspersions on earlier generations.10

notes_en.en: It is agreed that there is no prohibition regarding sheratzim that are seen through a microscope or magnifying glass, for the Torah was not given to the ministering angels but to human beings, according to their power of sight (Binat Adam 34:49; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 84:36; Igrot Moshe YD 2:146; Yabi'a Omer vol. 4, YD 21; Shevet Ha-levi 7:122). However, the definition of sight according to this division is unclear, since against a contrasting background one can see a tiny sheretz that under other conditions can be seen only with a microscope. For example, in small printed fonts, the size of the period at the end of a sentence is about a fifth of a millimeter, and it is visible because it is on a contrasting background. Likewise, experts with excellent eyesight sometimes see, even against a non-contrasting background, sheratzim that others see only with a magnifying glass. (See Bedikat Ha-mazon Ka-halakha by Rav Vaye, vol. 1 pp. 213-223.)

The stringent authorities learned from the words of a number of Aḥaronim who warned that certain foods must be checked well by people with good eyesight and under good conditions, that one must search and check even for very tiny sheratzim that ordinary people have difficulty finding, and which they can see only when they are pointed out. However, when one examines their words closely, it seems that there are degrees of stringency among them, and it is possible that some of them only intended to warn about noticeable sheratzim that people of reasonable eyesight see naturally.
From the words of the sages of Aram Tzova (Aleppo), the rabbinic dynasty of the Laniado family, and Rabbi Ḥayim Abulafia, one can learn the approach of the stringent, for they decreed not to eat grape leaves because "they found in them small worms, extremely thin, withered and blasted by the east wind, which the eye can hardly discern, lying and pressed into the veins of the leaves, intertwined and entangled in the corners; and most of those checking will find nothing in them and will see them as smooth and clean; and when the experts and those of strong sight come in their place, after much scrutiny they stir them with the point of a needle, and they begin to walk on the leaves; while still walking they hide in one of the hollows among the points of the protruding ridges and vanish from the eye, and they are not found again" (cited in Responsa Masat Moshe 4). Some disagreed with them and permitted grape leaves with a good checking or rubbing, as cited in Responsa Re'aḥ Sadeh 9, in the name of his father, Maharash Dweck. The Ḥida (Maḥazik Berakha YD 84:24) also leaned toward their view.
The Maharam ben Ḥaviv (Responsa Kol Gadol 5) wrote about vinegar in which thin worms grow that are forbidden by Torah law, and even after five strainings some of them remain "that swarm at the bottom of the vessel. And they are thinner than a hair, having no substance except the swarming that is discernible in them in sunlight," and straining helps for them only after cooking (for then they cannot pass through the strainer). The Pri Ḥadash 84:34 is also mentioned as one of the stringent authorities; he wrote: "The essence of the checking in this is to hold up each and every leaf against the sun, and the worm will be seen; and sometimes it is not seen, and one must feel with the hands to find it." And this was recorded as halakha in Pri Ha-adama and Ḥesed La-alafim.
Similarly, the Ben Ish Ḥai wrote (Tzav 27): "The women should be careful in checking the ḥazeret (lettuce) and the karpas, for for every worm there is liability of five sets of lashes… It once happened that a certain sage entered a courtyard on Erev Pesaḥ and saw the woman of the house with two large baskets full of ḥazeret before her, and she was washing the leaves of the ḥazeret and looking at them quickly, offhandedly, and placing them in the basket before her. The sage said to her: How many hairs are on your head? She said to him: I have not counted them, and in my opinion it is impossible to count them. He said to her: The hairs of your head can be counted, but the liability of lashes that is on your neck cannot be counted…" And he suggested that she take only the stalks. (However, what he wrote about "lashes" is by way of exaggeration, for in practice they did not become liable to lashes, since they ate unintentionally and without witnesses and warning.)
Some were slightly less stringent, as the Shela wrote (Sha'ar Ha-otiyot, Kedushat Ha-akhila 18) regarding the checking of various fruits and legumes, "that the one checking them must have good and fine eyesight, for several times people checked and said that there were none of them there, and another observer came and showed everyone how there were very, very many of them, beyond count, moving and stirring. Therefore the obligation applies to look for this, for it is a Torah prohibition." However, he did not require that the checking be done against the sun; therefore it is reasonable that he meant to exclude a few people whose eyesight is weaker than normal, who did not see many sheratzim. And some were stringent but did not write it as an absolute obligation, as the MB 473:42 wrote (based on Ḥatam Sofer OḤ 132) about lettuce for maror: "Very commonly in the days of Pesaḥ there are small worms that are not discernible to those of weak eyesight; therefore, one who does not have special God-fearing people who will check it properly – it is better to take tamkha (horseradish), even though it is third in the order in which they are listed, for heaven forbid that one stumble in a negative commandment for the sake of fulfilling a rabbinic positive commandment, and especially since it is possible to fulfill both by means of tamkha." If the matter were forbidden by Torah law, they would not have used the expression "it is better," but would rather have decisively forbidden lettuce that was not checked properly; apparently, by the words "heaven forbid that one stumble in a negative commandment" they meant the prohibition of sheratzim in principle.
The ones who establish the stringent approach in our day are Rav Moshe Vaye, author of the series Bedikat Ha-mazon Ka-halakha, and Rav Shneur Z. Revaḥ, author of the series Tola'at Shani – Dinei Ḥarakim Ba-mazon (Laws of Insects in Food). In their books they detailed the obligation of checking for each fruit and vegetable, and the names of the tiny sheratzim commonly found in food, with magnified pictures of them. Among them: mites (a third of a millimeter): red ones are found on strawberries, and white ones in flour. Even the greatest experts see them only while they are crawling. Aphids – yellowish-green in color, half a millimeter to two millimeters in size. Thrips – an elongated insect, half a millimeter to a millimeter in size. As a larva its color is yellowish-white and it moves slowly, and when mature it is gray-black, jumps nimbly and hides in the folds of leaves such as lettuce, cabbage, cauliflower and corn kernels. Leaf miner – the leaf-miner fly lays tiny eggs inside the leaves, and from them hatch larvae 1-3 millimeters in size, which eat and crawl within the thickness of the leaves and finally exit the leaf and fall to the ground. These tunnels are visible in ordinary light, and against the light one can see a tiny larva at their end. Fly maggots – white worms with a tiny black dot at their head, between 1 and 8 millimeters. Moth larvae – cream-colored, found in dried foods, between 1 and 8 millimeters; they cause the formation of sticky silk webs and white crumbs. Weevil – an insect found in warehouses that swarms in rice and other legumes, about 4 millimeters; it is able to pierce nylon packaging and penetrate inside. Caterpillars such as Spodoptera, from about half a centimeter to five centimeters. Sometimes small flies, small spiders and small mosquitoes are also found in leafy vegetables, and in primitive agriculture they are more common. When a vegetable is taken out of the refrigerator, the sheratzim on it are dormant, and one needs to warm the leaves a little in front of the sun or a fire in order to see them. Another way to see tiny sheratzim found in dill and parsley is to shake them well over white or black paper.

The custom of most of the Jewish people and of many of the great Torah authorities was not to be so meticulous in checking food, and although those who examined it closely often found tiny sheratzim in it, they continued to instruct that food be checked with ordinary sight, without being meticulous in searching for tiny sheratzim. The basis of their reasoning is that the Torah was not given to the ministering angels but to human beings, and human beings do not discern the tiny sheratzim; as we find throughout the Torah, that in every matter we follow what people actually perceive. For example, in tasting a mixture, we follow the sense of an ordinary person (Rashba; Beit Yosef 98:1), and so wrote Rav Sherira Gaon regarding the measure of a kezayit for a final blessing (Peninei Halakha: Berakhot 10:5-6, n. 7).
And although they did not write this explicitly, this is proven from the Talmud, the Rishonim, the Rambam and the Shulḥan Arukh, who did not elaborate in detail on the laws of checking for sheratzim for each vegetable and fruit, as would have been fitting if this were indeed an obligation intended to prevent a Torah prohibition or even a rabbinic prohibition, just as they elaborated on all the other common food prohibitions. Nor did they set necessary guidelines for checking for sheratzim, such as that the sheratzim be checked against a background of contrasting color, that the checking always be done in sunlight and not inside houses, which were dim without large windows such as are customary in our day, and that people over the age of fifty should not check, since their eyesight weakens and they cannot see the tiny sheratzim. Nor did they require that experts deal with checking for sheratzim; rather they relied on the checking of every person, and only one in whose checked food a ḥomet was found (a small lizard according to Rav Sa'adya Gaon, and a snail according to Rashi) lost his presumption of reliability, for it is clearly visible to the eyes (SA 84:11). The poskim did not need to write this explicitly, for this was known through tradition. Therefore proofs can only be brought from the general tenor of their words, such as from the fact that the main halakhic discussions concern large sheratzim, as opposed to the tiny sheratzim about which the stringent are meticulous today. For example, the Rashba (1:275) warned about the larva in beans, even though it is "very, very small," and yet it is ten to a hundred times larger than the tiny sheratzim. Likewise they dealt with ants (SA 84:12-13), or with flour worms (milvin), whose size is between half a centimeter and three centimeters (below, n. 21). This is also proven from the words of the stringent authorities, who complained about the people, who did not check properly, and about the rabbis, who did not instruct them to check properly (as cited in the Harḥavot). Similarly, the Pri Ḥadash wrote (84:9) that out of concern for sheratzim that left the cooked dish, one should examine it by day, or at night by the light of "a torch or many candles," and the tiny sheratzim cannot be seen by a torch or many candles. Moreover, it is not possible that they intended to be stringent about tiny sheratzim, since in practice they could not properly clean food of them. For when they checked lettuce and cabbage leaves, since there was no running water in houses, they could check them only by sight, without rinsing under a stream of water, and in practice rinsing is often more effective than meticulous checking. Likewise regarding the demand of the stringent to sift with a 70-mesh silk sieve: such sieves did not exist in the past (as cited below, n. 21). It should be added that even in the words of many of the Aḥaronim who warned about small sheratzim, on whom the stringent rely, it is possible to understand that they meant larger sheratzim, which are discernible to the eye in ordinary light, "and one must feel with the hands to find it" (in the words of the Pri Ḥadash, who was mentioned as one of the stringent), and not as the stringent understood them.
Some of the stringent claim that in the days of the Talmud and the Rishonim tiny sheratzim were not common, and they became widespread following the extensive trade that began to take place between different countries, including America, which brought sheratzim with it from place to place (see Or Ha-ḥayim, Vayikra 11:43). However, although following intercontinental trade the number of common species of sheratzim increased everywhere, it is reasonable that in practice the number of sheratzim swarming on each fruit and vegetable did not increase, since they multiply according to the amount of food available to them. The stringent also claim that today the sheratzim cling to fruits and vegetables more strongly and are also tinier, but it is difficult to accept this claim without supporting evidence. The stringent further claim that in the past most people engaged in agriculture and knew how to discern sheratzim like the experts of our day, and the halakha was determined according to them. However, since they did not require checking all foods against the sun, even experts could not discern the tiny sheratzim. In addition, it is reasonable that the farmers were interested in the sheratzim that damaged their fields and not in the other tiny sheratzim. It seems that reality is the opposite of the claim of the stringent: today vegetables coming from modern agriculture are much cleaner of sheratzim visible to the eye, since consumers demand clean, high-quality produce, whereas in the past sheratzim were more common, just as even today they are more common in primitive cultivation, such as the vegetables grown in Arab villages in Judea and Samaria, in which many sheratzim visible to the eye are found. Apparently most of the warnings of the stringent were stated with regard to such produce. For it is clear that one should not eat lettuce containing small flies and small spiders, and all they asked was that the lettuce be checked seriously by people whose eyesight is good, and not hastily or in the dim light that there was in houses. In addition, under the living conditions of the past, when domestic and other animals were raised near the houses, lice swarmed in abundance, and the houses were not paved, many worms often swarmed in the food, and it was within such a reality that the stringent said their words.
Accordingly, there are no firm sources in the words of the poskim for the approach of the stringent (except for the sages of Aram Tzova and a few other individuals), and certainly their approach contradicts tradition. However, apparently their position took shape and grew stronger in the period of the Aḥaronim as a result of two factors: a) the development of scientific and research instruments, such as the magnifying glass, eyeglasses and the microscope, which made it possible to see the tiny sheratzim well; b) in modern society every field has become the special domain of experts, and so too those who deal with sheratzim learned to recognize the tiniest ones, to photograph them and to illustrate them through books and films. And since they have become familiar and known, it is difficult to ignore them. However, the lenient hold that these changes did not create a new law according to which one must be stringent and check for tiny sheratzim, since even today ordinary people do not see the tiny sheratzim and are not aware of their existence.
Leaning toward the opinion of the lenient: Igrot Moshe YD 4:2; Rav Kassar in Ha-ḥayim Ve-ha-shalom YD 16; Minḥat Shlomo 2:61; Si'aḥ Naḥum 45; Shema Shlomo vol. 7, YD 4; Rav Bigel in Ekhol Be-simḥa p. 196; Rav Weitman, Emunat Itekha 37; Rav Shaul David Botschko, Be-ikvot Ha-meḥaber vol. 2 pp. 269ff.; the book Lakhem Yihyeh Le-okhla by Rav Eitam Henkin, may God avenge his blood.

sections.title_en: The Halakha Follows the Lenient Opinion
sections.body_en:
As for the halakha, it seems that one should decide in accordance with the opinion of the lenient, that there is no need to check for tiny sheratzim that people do not see with ordinary sight. There are five main foundations for this, on the basis of each one of which one can decide in accordance with the opinion of the lenient; all the more so when they are combined:

a) The discussion concerns a rabbinic prohibition, since by Torah law, as long as the taste of the sheratzim cannot be sensed, they are nullified in the food in which they are found. It was the Sages who were stringent and established that a beria is not nullified even in a thousand; consequently, when there is a dispute whether one must check for tiny sheratzim, one should rule according to the lenient opinion.11

b) Even if we follow the approach of the stringent, that one must check for tiny sheratzim, according to several of the great Rishonim, if there is a thousand times their amount against them, they are nullified. For the stringency of the Sages is that a beria is not nullified in sixty, but in close to a thousand it is nullified. And several of the great Aḥaronim wrote that in case of need one may rely on them. All the more so when dealing with tiny, repulsive sheratzim that have no importance.12

c) Since there is a dispute over the status of tiny sheratzim, in everything relating to the definition of a "common minority" one should rule according to the lenient opinions; consequently, generally there are no sheratzim at the level of a "common minority," and there is no need to check for them, since we follow the majority.13

d) It is reasonable that a Torah eating prohibition cannot take effect on a food whose taste and swallowing cannot be sensed when it is eaten by itself. In practice, it is impossible to sense the taste and swallowing of tiny sheratzim such as thrips and mites. It does seem that a person who sees them and nevertheless eats them transgresses a rabbinic prohibition. But as long as he has not seen them, he has committed no prohibition.14

e) Even if it is a sheretz such that, if one ate it by itself and concentrated, he could sense its taste and swallowing, and would consequently transgress a Torah prohibition – when there is a doubt whether it is present within another food, and while eating that food the taste of the sheretz cannot be sensed, there is no prohibition in eating it. For with each bite he eats, he does not know whether he also ate a sheretz, and this is akin to a "davar she-eino mitkaven" (an unintended act).15

notes_en.en: The sheratzim hidden in foods, which are hard to find, are considered mixed into them, and by Torah law they are nullified in sixty, as wrote Knesset Ha-gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef 84:61; Ohel Yosef (by Rabbi Yosef Molkho) YD 21; Tzemaḥ Tzedek of Lubavitch YD 70; Aryeh De-vei Ila'i OḤ 6; Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, third edition, 2:32; Avnei Nezer YD 156; Ḥavalim Ba-ne'imim 4:22; Ḥazon Ish YD 14:1, 6, and others. And so emerges from the words of all the countless poskim who dealt with the definitions of the nullification of a beria and did not consider that since the sheretz can be found with great effort, it is not nullified. However, some hold that any sheretz that can be found, even if this involves great difficulty, is not considered mixed, and consequently even by Torah law it is not nullified in sixty (Pri To'ar 84:15; Kereti 19; Ḥokhmat Adam 51:1; Yeshu'ot Ya'akov 84:5; Ziv'ḥei Tzedek 98; Yeshu'ot Malko YD 13). And it is possible that even according to their approach, tiny sheratzim that are not discernible to an ordinary person are considered mixed and are nullified.

Even when it is clear that tiny sheratzim are mixed into the food, which are nullified by Torah law (as explained in the previous note), according to many poskim they are nullified by rabbinic law as well, for various reasons (as explained above, n. 5). a) Some hold that a beria is nullified in 960 (Rash, Or Zaru'a and Rashba), and their opinion is combined to be lenient (Pleti 100:2; Mishkenot Ya'akov YD 36; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 100:15; Rav Pe'alim vol. 4, YD 8). b) Some hold that the Sages decreed that a beria is not nullified because of its importance, but when it is tiny and not visible to an ordinary glance, it has no importance and is nullified (Mishkenot Ya'akov YD 36; Ḥokhmat Shlomo 84:1; Yad Yehuda; Ḥazon Ish YD 14:6-7; Le-horot Natan 12:63; Ḥavalim Ba-ne'imim 4:22; Igrot Moshe YD 4:2; Rav Rabinovitch). c) Some say that repulsive sheratzim have no importance and are nullified in sixty (Tiferet Le-Moshe 103:1; Rav Kalischer in Tzvi La-tzaddik; Ktav Sofer YD 63; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 100:17-18; Hit'orerut Teshuva 4:36, and others).

As we learned in n. 6, a food in which a sheretz is found in most cases is considered presumed to contain sheratzim and must be checked. And if one is found at the level of a "common minority," it must be checked, but if one did not check and it can no longer be checked, it is permitted to eat. According to the Rivash, a "common minority" is between about 25% and 49%, and according to Mishkenot Ya'akov and those who agree with him, above 10%. Likewise, regarding the unit of measurement there are several possibilities, and according to the lenient approach it is a bite. Consequently, there is almost no food, including leafy vegetables, in which sheratzim would be found in a "common minority" according to the approach of the Rivash with a unit of measurement of a bite. And since the entire attitude toward tiny sheratzim is disputed, on the question of defining a "common minority" one should rule according to the lenient approach; all the more so since even according to the intermediate approaches in defining a "common minority" there would be no obligation to check. To this one should add the opinion of those who hold that when it is difficult to check, there is no obligation to check in a case of a "common minority" (above, n. 6).

We learned in Ḥullin 103b that according to Rabbi Yoḥanan the essence of eating is the enjoyment of the throat, that is, the enjoyment of the palate; and according to Reish Lakish, the enjoyment of the stomach. The halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 14:3). Similarly, Aḥi'ezer 3:81 wrote that eating that involves no enjoyment of the throat and stomach involves no Torah prohibition. However, it is reasonable that if one sees the sheretz and swallows it, even though he does not sense its taste and swallowing, he transgresses a rabbinic prohibition, similar to the law of "aḥshevei" (he has deemed it significant) that was stated regarding foods that have become unfit for human consumption (Rosh; Terumat Ha-deshen 129; Taz 442:8; below ch. 34, n. 8). But one who eats them unwittingly does not transgress a prohibition even by rabbinic law. Similarly, they permitted eating a burnt sheretz for medicinal purposes, since its taste has been nullified, and the poskim disagreed whether it is permitted to eat it ordinarily, because of aḥshevei or bal teshaktzu (SA 84:17, and commentaries).

Since the prohibition of eating a sheretz is committed with one bite and swallow, in all doubts regarding awareness of the prohibition we go by each bite separately (and see SA 109:1). If so, when with each and every bite there is a doubt whether a sheretz is mixed in whose taste cannot be sensed and which is not wanted, this is a "safek pesik reisha" (a doubtful inevitable consequence), which according to many, regarding Shabbat, is considered a "davar she-eino mitkaven," which involves no prohibition (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 9, n. 2); and this is the opinion of many regarding all prohibitions (She'ilat Shmuel 34:3; Maharshag 8:151; Ḥelkat Ya'akov YD 211; Yeshu'at Moshe 4:25; Igrot Moshe YD 1:39). However, when it is a large sheretz whose taste can be sensed, this reasoning cannot be applied, since in practice he senses it while eating and unavoidably derives enjoyment. Shivat Tziyon 28 wrote similarly regarding ordinary sheratzim, and Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach wrote something similar regarding sheratzim that are very hard to find (Minḥat Shlomo 1:6; 2:61).
In addition to the five foundations mentioned above, there are two more foundations for leniency: f) Safek sefeika: even one who does not accept the principle that this is a rabbinic doubt, on the basis of foundations a and d, and who even casts doubt on the other foundations, can generally be lenient because of safek sefeika: a) perhaps the halakha follows those who hold that one need not search for sheratzim that are not visible to an ordinary glance; b) even if he checked with some negligence, perhaps in practice his checking was effective and there is no sheretz there (see Kereti 84:19); c) perhaps the halakha follows the lenient in defining a "common minority" (above, n. 6); d) and if it is a food meant to be cooked, an additional doubt is combined: perhaps a limb fell off it, or it was crushed and lost its form and was nullified in sixty (Rashba); e) if the sheretz grew in an attached fruit and did not leave it, one should combine the approach of some Rishonim who were lenient about this, as cited in n. 4.
g) Some hold that the obligation of checking in a "common minority" was established regarding adhesions of the lung because the adhesions are very noticeable, and consequently "if he does not check, it appears as if he is turning a blind eye to the prohibition" (Rashba, Ḥullin 9a, in the name of his teacher Rabbenu Yona); which is not the case with sheratzim, which are not noticeable.

sections.title_en: The Practical Halakha and the Approach of the Mehadrin
sections.body_en:
As we learned, on the basis of several foundations, the main halakha follows the opinion of the lenient. However, the opinion of the stringent also has a place in our day, since it is based on modern research methods and measuring instruments, which have heightened in our awareness the presence of tiny sheratzim in vegetables and foods. And it can be implemented thanks to developments in science and technology that have provided tools for dealing with tiny sheratzim, such as the development of soaps and cleaning agents, by means of which vegetables can be cleaned of sheratzim; and likewise the development of refrigerators in which vegetables and food can be kept without tiny sheratzim developing in them. Methods have also been developed by which most vegetables and fruits can be grown in conditions in which tiny sheratzim do not develop. Following this, many rabbis in recent generations instructed to be meticulous (lehadder) in accordance with the approach of the stringent. It is even correct to say that the ordinary actions that people do in order to clean vegetables and fruits, such as soaking and rinsing, are proper to do for the purpose of removing tiny sheratzim. But when this involves great effort or significant financial expense, one should return to the rules of halakha and rule according to the opinion of those who permit.

Thus, generally there are three approaches in halakha: a) kosher, according to the basic halakha; b) the middle way: cleaning the vegetables and fruits by soaking them in water with a dissolving agent, and rinsing; c) the approach of the stringent, for those who wish to be meticulous. In the following halakhot we will explain, regarding various foods, the halakha according to the different approaches.

It is worth noting that in factories and large kitchens it is sometimes necessary to be more stringent than in a private home, because a breach in a large kitchen may cause hundreds and thousands to stumble. In addition, the temptation to violate the halakha in them is greater, both on the part of the business owner, who can earn a great deal of money from it, and on the part of the workers, who sometimes, because of the heavy workload, have difficulty carrying out the required checks and cleaning. Also, storage conditions in kitchens and factories are sometimes less good, and they lead to the development of more insects. Therefore, in order to ensure that they reach the basic kashrut required by halakha, it is often necessary to instruct factories and large kitchens according to the approach of the stringent, and in the process they gain by rising to a mehadrin level of kashrut.

sections.title_en: Leafy Vegetables – The Approach of the Stringent
sections.body_en:
The problem with leafy vegetables, such as lettuce, cabbage, parsley, dill, coriander, artichoke, asparagus, spinach and mint, is that during their growth tiny sheratzim such as thrips and aphids are attracted to them. Ordinary sheratzim also sometimes swarm on them, but they are visible to the eye and come off with ordinary rinsing. However, the tiny sheratzim whose color is similar to the color of the leaf are very hard to see, and even soaking in water with vinegar or soap and rinsing, which removes many sheratzim, does not remove all the tiny sheratzim, as has been found in laboratory tests. Therefore, according to their approach, it is forbidden to eat these vegetables unless a God-fearing person who knows the sheratzim well and whose eyesight is good examines each and every leaf calmly against the sun or a light table and removes all the tiny sheratzim from them. And since such checking is difficult to carry out, according to the approach of the stringent there are in practice two ways of obtaining vegetables that are presumed clean of sheratzim:

The first method was invented in Gush Katif under the guidance of the rabbis of the Torah Ve-ha-aretz Institute, whereby vegetables clean of sheratzim are grown in insulated greenhouses. For this purpose the soil is disinfected of sheratzim and of sheretz eggs, and the greenhouse is sealed with mesh sheets, which allow air and sunlight to enter and block sheratzim. Also, from time to time the vegetables are sprayed with insecticides, while the reliable companies, such as Ḥasalat, take care not to spray beyond what is permitted by health regulations. Despite all the precautions and the great investment, and to a certain extent because of the spraying restrictions, sheratzim sometimes manage to penetrate the greenhouse and multiply in it at the rate of a "common minority," and then the entire crop loses its presumption of being clean of tiny sheratzim according to the approach of the stringent. Therefore the price of these vegetables is much higher than the price of ordinary vegetables.

The second method is growing the vegetables in cold places, so that throughout their growth the temperature does not rise above 14 degrees. In such a climate sheratzim do not multiply, and the vegetables are presumed clean of sheratzim. This method is convenient to use abroad, in cold places. However, in Israel there are no places that cold; nevertheless, with controlled spraying they succeed in growing vegetables in open fields in winter with very few tiny sheratzim, and by rinsing the vegetables they succeed in reaching a state in which the chance that there are sheratzim in the vegetables is low, to the point that even according to the approach of most of the stringent, the vegetables are presumed clean of sheratzim.

sections.title_en: The Halakha and the Middle Way for Leafy Vegetables
sections.body_en:
According to the basic halakha, one may suffice with a good rinsing of leafy vegetables in water and looking at them with an ordinary glance, and if one sees a sheretz on them, removing it. However, as we learned (in halakha 8), it is proper to follow the middle way and perform an action which, if there are sheratzim on the leaves, would presumably remove them. For this purpose one should soak the vegetables for about four minutes in water with a dissolving agent such as salt or vinegar, and rinse them under running water, so that if there are sheratzim on the leaves, soaking them in water with a dissolving agent will loosen the adhesive that strengthens their grip on the leaves, and rinsing them in water will remove the sheratzim from the leaves. Often this action removes all the tiny sheratzim or reduces them to less than the level of a "common minority," and then it is effective even according to the approach of the stringent. In terms of removing the sheratzim, it is preferable to soak the leaves in water with soap, which has been found more effective than vinegar or salt, but some are concerned that soap is not healthy. There are natural agents such as Sterili, which have been found as effective as soap and without any health concern.

One should make sure that both when soaking the leaves and when rinsing them, the water reaches all the folds and crevices in the leaves. Therefore, with vegetables such as lettuce, cabbage and artichoke, one must separate the leaves so that the water can get in between them. For although lettuce and cabbage reach us closed, at the beginning of their growth they are open, and then sheratzim can penetrate the inner leaves. When one intends to cut the leaves for a salad, it is preferable to first cut them into the pieces desired for the salad and afterward soak and rinse them, because the more they are cut, the more easily the water reaches all the places in them.

Sometimes leafy vegetables are of poor quality, and then they are full of small and large sheratzim that are clearly visible to the eye, and in order to clean them one must rinse them again and again until they are clean of sheratzim.16

notes_en.en:
The stringent claim that even soaking in water with a dissolving agent such as vinegar, salt or soap, and rinsing, does not completely remove all the tiny sheratzim. However, as we learned, the main halakha is that there is no need to search for tiny sheratzim that are not discernible with an ordinary glance. And according to the middle way, it is proper to remove what can be removed in the ordinary way, without special effort. It should be added that generally, in this manner one reaches vegetables cleaner than what the Aḥaronim demanded according to the approach of the stringent. For they demanded that people with good eyesight and fear of Heaven check the lettuce, and generally, by soaking in water with soap or vinegar or salt and rinsing well under running water, which did not exist in the past, one reaches a better result.
Soap dissolves fats well, and consequently also the adhesive on the legs of the sheratzim. One who is concerned that even after rinsing, soap residues will remain in the pores of the vegetables and harm his health can instead use vinegar or salt, which, although less effective than soap, are also effective in removing tiny sheratzim; and whatever perhaps does not come off involves no prohibition, as we learned in halakha 7. Some hold that even from a health standpoint it is preferable to soak leafy vegetables in water with soap, because just as soap is effective in removing sheratzim, so it is effective in removing pesticide residue, which is more dangerous than soap, and after good rinsing the soap and the pesticide come off. Best of all is to use natural agents such as Sterili, which on the one hand cause no health damage at all, and on the other hand dissolve the pesticide and the adhesive on the legs of the sheratzim like soap.
Sometimes the leaves of lettuce or cabbage have a "leaf miner" (as cited in n. 9), and according to the stringent one must look at the leaf against the light to check whether it has a tunnel at the end of which there is a maggot 1-3 millimeters long that must be removed. However, as we learned, the main halakha is that there is no need to check for it, because this is a rare phenomenon, and even if one sees a tunnel, it is not clear that there is a maggot in it, since at the end of the process it exits the leaf and falls to the ground. Moreover, if it developed in the detached plant, according to all opinions it involves no prohibition; and if it developed while attached, according to some of the Rishonim, as long as it has not left it involves no prohibition (as explained in n. 4). Seaweed – sometimes water sheratzim such as tiny crustaceans are found among the fronds of the seaweed. However, even according to the stringent, soaking it in water with soap and rinsing it removes them.

sections.body_en:
There are vegetables in which tiny sheratzim are commonly found and it is impossible to remove all of them by rinsing or checking. Such is the situation with cauliflower and broccoli, a significant part of which is florets, inside which the tiny sheratzim hide, and it is impossible to see them without completely taking the flower apart and checking all its small parts for a long time. Even soaking in soapy water and rinsing is not sufficiently effective, since the stream of water does not reach with force the places where they hide, and consequently it cannot remove all of them. According to the stringent, the only way to eat them from ordinary cultivation is to throw away the florets, which are about forty percent of the vegetable, and eat the remaining stalks after good rinsing; or to consume cauliflower and broccoli grown under special conditions in which sheratzim do not develop.

However, as we learned, according to the rules of halakha there is no need to check for the tiny sheratzim; rather it is enough to rinse them well, and as long as no sheratzim are seen on them, it is permitted to eat them. It is more proper to soak them in water with a dissolving agent for about four minutes and rinse them well under a stream of water.

However, unlike lettuce and other leafy vegetables, which often, after soaking and rinsing, contain no tiny sheratzim or fewer than the level of a "common minority," with cauliflower and broccoli soaking and rinsing do not succeed in achieving such good results. However, since cauliflower and broccoli are cooked, and sometimes the sheretz dissolves in cooking and drops from the level of a beria, this can be regarded as the middle way (as explained in n. 17).

sections.title_en: Corn on the Cob, Strawberries and Green Onions
sections.body_en:
Corn on the cob: According to the stringent, it is forbidden to eat the kernels while they are still on the cob, since tiny sheratzim (thrips) sometimes hide between them, and the only way to eat them from ordinary cultivation is to cut the corn kernels off the cob and rinse them, to ensure that there are no tiny sheratzim among them. However, according to the rules of halakha, and also according to the middle way, since an ordinary person does not see them, and it is doubtful whether they are present, and in addition they undergo cooking, it is enough to rinse the cob.17

Green onion and leek leaves: According to the stringent, one must cut each leaf in two, soak it in water with soap and rinse it while rubbing it along its entire length, because of tiny sheratzim that are sometimes found in it. According to the rules of halakha, one need not be concerned about tiny sheratzim that an ordinary person does not see. And according to the middle way, one should cut off about three centimeters from the point of connection between the bulb and the leaf and throw it away, since in this area the concern is greater, and separate the rest of the leaves, soak them in water with a dissolving agent and rinse, without cutting each leaf in two.

On strawberries there are sometimes tiny mites, about a third of a millimeter in diameter, which hide in the pits of the tiny seeds on their skin. According to the stringent, it is forbidden to eat strawberries from ordinary cultivation unless their skin is peeled, or they are soaked in water with a dissolving agent and rinsed while thoroughly brushing their skin. However, according to the rules of halakha, since an ordinary person does not see these tiny mites, there is no need to search for them. And according to the middle way, one should cut off the place where the strawberry is attached to the stem, soak them in water with a dissolving agent and rinse them well. This should also be done with raspberries and mulberries.18

notes_en.en: The insects found in corn are thrips, which are light in color at first and dark when mature; their length is between half a millimeter and one millimeter. In summer they are more common. According to what we learned in n. 6 on the topic of a "common minority": according to the lenient, in winter they do not reach a "common minority," and in summer they sometimes do. And according to the stringent, in winter they reach a "common minority," and in summer even a majority. But these are tiny sheratzim that are not discernible to the eye of one looking with an ordinary glance, and as we learned (in halakha 7), there is no need to check for them. Even according to the middle way it is possible to eat them after rinsing alone, since they are cooked in any case, and another doubt is combined: perhaps in cooking they dissolved and dropped from the level of a beria and are nullified in sixty (as in the words of the Rashba cited in n. 7).

On strawberries the stringent sometimes found a "red mite" (a tiny spider mite), about a third of a millimeter in size, and they even publicized this in magnified videos. However, almost all the people who searched for a mite on a strawberry did not find one. Only with special lighting are they sometimes seen. Therefore, there is no obligation to be concerned about them. However, since it is good to clean fruit in any case, according to the middle way it is good to do so.

sections.body_en:
There are fruits, such as figs, guavas, dates and apricots, in which sheratzim are sometimes found, and therefore before eating them one should open them and check them. With fresh and dried figs one must look carefully, because sometimes the sheratzim resemble the internal form of the fig. However, one need not be concerned about what most people do not see. Likewise, worms are found in guava fruit, and one should cut it into quarters in order to check it. Likewise, one should examine any fruit that has rot in it, lest there be sheratzim around the rot.

In various nuts, such as cashew nuts, there are sometimes sheratzim, and the sign of this is white webs or signs of gnawing. Sometimes the sheratzim only swarm around the fruit, and then, if one removes the webs and the nut remains whole and nice, it may be eaten.

Packaged dried fruits, such as raisins: if they have webs or powder that crumbled from them, it is a sign that they are infested with sheratzim, and they must be checked well; and sometimes it is preferable to throw them away, because checking them is difficult.19

Scale insects: Sometimes there are black dots on the peel of oranges and citrus fruits, created by tiny scale insects (0.2-0.6 mm) that crawled on the peel, settled in place and secreted a substance to protect themselves. The poskim disagreed about their law. Some are stringent and hold that since the covering of the scale insect is visible to all, and one can also discern the sheretz itself while it is crawling, those preparing food from orange peels must remove them. Likewise, when peeling an orange, one must take care that the scale insects do not stick to one's fingers and pass from them to the orange or to other foods (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, cited in Shemirat Shabbat Ke-hilkhata 3, n. 117). And some permit and hold that one need not be concerned about them, since without the protective layer an ordinary person would not see them, and even if he saw them, he would think it was a tiny bit of dirt; all the more so when in practice one sees a black dot on the peel and there is a doubt whether it is dirt or the covering of a scale insect (Shevet Ha-levi 7:122). And even when it is known that the dot is the covering of a scale insect, this does not necessarily mean that the insect is still there, for over time the males go on their way, and the females disintegrate until they can no longer be considered a beria. In practice, the main view is that of the lenient.

notes_en.en: As a rule, when there are sheratzim in dates, the taste of the date also changes for the worse. However, sometimes there is an infection in dates that causes a blackening called "paiḥat," whose taste is very bad, but there are no sheratzim in it. According to the approach of the stringent, one who is not expert in figs and in the tiny sheratzim found in them should refrain from eating them. And regarding dates, one must check them against a light source.

sections.body_en:
In grain, rice and legumes, sheratzim are sometimes found that developed among the grains while they were in the fields or in warehouses. The higher the quality of the crop, and the cleaner and colder the place where it is stored, for a short time, the lower the chance that it will contain sheratzim. Since consumers today demand clean products, storage conditions have been improved and storage time shortened; therefore, when one buys products of reliable companies from clean stores, there is no need to check them for sheratzim, since the concern that sheratzim will be found in them is below the level of a "common minority" according to all opinions (above, n. 6). Only in a case where one sees a change in the bag that arouses suspicion that perhaps it was kept in an unclean place or for too long should one check a sample of it. If the sample is clean, there is no need to check the rest. If a sheretz is found in it, the entire contents of the bag must be checked. When one sees moth webs, or crumbs and powder, in the package, there is a high likelihood that there are sheratzim in it, and it must be checked thoroughly. Today food companies are careful about the cleanliness of their products and are willing to replace a product infested with sheratzim with a clean product; and when there is no urgent need for the product, it is preferable to replace it rather than take the trouble of checking it.

However, those who buy grains and legumes in bulk, or in old bags, or from stores that are not careful about cleanliness, may find sheratzim in them at the level of a "common minority," and they should be checked by spreading them out over a surface.

Chickpeas and beans: There are two concerns with chickpeas, beans and similar species. a) As with all kinds of grain, sheratzim sometimes swarm among them. b) Sometimes flies and gnats lay eggs inside them, which develop into larvae that eventually break through their outer skin and fly away. From the outside these larvae look like a black circle; when one presses on both sides of it, the larva is squeezed out and sometimes even moves a little.20 Since the larvae cannot be seen while the legumes are dry, one should soak them in boiling water for about half an hour, or in lukewarm water for about eight hours, so that their outer skin becomes transparent and the grains can be checked.

When one buys these legumes in bags of reliable companies that were stored in clean places, there is no need to check them, since they are presumed clean; rather it is enough to look at them to see that they are clean in the usual way. However, if the bags stayed on the shelf for a long time or were stored in a dirty place, or if they are produced by less reliable companies or were bought in bulk, they must be checked well. When a doubt arises regarding a bag from a reliable company that perhaps was not kept properly, one should check a sample of it, and if a sheretz is found there, all of it should be checked.

notes_en.en: As we learned in n. 4, the ruling follows the majority of the Rishonim, who hold that sheratzim that developed in a fruit attached to the ground (by way of the tree or plant) are forbidden. But when the worm has no room to crawl, such as the larva that develops in a fruit without crawling in it, some are lenient, among them: Maharam of Rothenburg, Rosh, Rabbenu Yeruḥam, Hagahot Maimoniyot, and SA 84:6. And some forbid, among them: Ramban, Rashba and Ran.
