And some were lenient like the SA because it is a safek sefeika: perhaps the halakha follows those who hold that even sheratzim that grow in an attached fruit are permitted; and if the halakha does not follow them, perhaps if it did not crawl inside the fruit it is permitted (Rabbi Refael Berdugo in Torot Emet 84; Halikhot Olam vol. 6, Naso 2). The opinion of most Aḥaronim is to be stringent (Shakh, Taz, Pri Ḥadash, Ḥokhmat Adam, Arukh Ha-shulḥan). And although one who wishes to be lenient and not check for the larvae may do so, since most of the Aḥaronim were stringent, it is proper ab initio to check a sample of produce that is not supervised.

sections.body_en:
Flour in which sheratzim developed: as long as they have not left the flour, they are not forbidden, for their law is like that of detached fruits in which sheratzim developed, which, as long as they have not left the fruit, are not forbidden (above, halakha 3). However, when sheratzim are seen in the flour and it is likely that they left and returned, according to most of the Rishonim we are concerned that they left, and they are forbidden. But the poskim disagreed whether one must check ordinary flour in which no sheratzim are seen. According to many, because of a safek sefeika there is no obligation to check it: the first doubt, perhaps there are no sheratzim in it; the second doubt, even if sheratzim are found in it, perhaps they did not leave and are not forbidden (Taz, Knesset Ha-gedola, Shulḥan Gavo'ah, and others). And some say that since sheratzim are sometimes found in flour, and it is possible to check it and resolve the doubt, it should be checked and one should not rely on the safek sefeika (Pleti and Minḥat Ya'akov). And indeed the Jewish people have customarily sifted flour. But all agree that if unsifted flour was baked or cooked, the baked good or dish is kosher.

The stringent require sifting the flour with a silk sieve with tiny holes of 70 mesh (70 holes per square inch), because sometimes there are tiny sheratzim in flour called "flour mites," whose size is slightly larger than a grain of flour, and only with a dense silk sieve can they be sifted out. However, according to halakha, and even according to the middle way, one may sift the flour with an ordinary sieve of about 30 mesh. For in addition to the fact that the main view is that of those who hold that one need not be concerned about such tiny sheratzim, as long as the sheratzim have not left the flour they are not forbidden, and with these tiny sheratzim there is no concern that they left the flour and returned.21

notes_en.en:
There is no prohibition regarding worms that developed in flour and did not leave it, just as there is no prohibition regarding worms that developed in a detached fruit and did not leave it (as explained above in halakha 3 and n. 4). Some hold that as long as we have not seen that they left and returned, there is no need to be concerned about the sheratzim seen in flour (Roke'aḥ 461; Sha'arei Dura 54; Agudda). And according to most poskim, when there is a concern that they left and returned, they are forbidden (Rosh, Maharaḥ Or Zaru'a, SA 84:5, Shakh, Taz, Pleti, Arukh Ha-shulḥan). And some hold that if the flour is in a vessel, there is no concern that they left, for even if they went out of the flour and crawled on the inner side of the vessel, they are still considered as not having left and are not forbidden (Pri Ḥadash 84:17; and see Noda Bi-Yehuda, first edition, YD 27; Halikhot Olam vol. 6, Naso 6). Admittedly, the Pri To'ar and Ḥokhmat Adam were stringent, holding that even if they crawled within the flour they are forbidden, since every particle of flour is a fruit in itself; but all the Rishonim and the overwhelming majority of the Aḥaronim do not agree with them (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 84:45-46).
The Aḥaronim disagreed whether one must sift ordinary flour that perhaps contains sheratzim. According to many it is not necessary, because of a safek sefeika: a) perhaps there are no sheratzim in it; b) and if there are, perhaps they did not leave (Taz 84:12; Knesset Ha-gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef 47; Shulḥan Gavo'ah 2; Simḥat Kohen YD 1:149). And a safek sefeika is permitted even where there is a concern of a Torah prohibition. On the other hand, some say that one must check the flour, because in several laws we find that when the concern is common and it is possible to check, one is not lenient and does not refrain from checking on the basis of the argument of safek sefeika (Pleti 84:7; Minḥat Ya'akov 80:4, 14; Shevet Ha-levi 7:125; see Maggid Mishneh, Hilkhot Ḥametz U-matza 2:10; SA OḤ 437:2; MB 9). Some Aḥaronim testified that in their locale sheratzim were usually found in flour, and then even according to most poskim the flour must be checked (Kaf Ha-ḥayim 84:63). In practice, the rabbis in recent generations instructed that flour be sifted, since sheratzim were often found in it.
But all agree that if unsifted flour was baked or cooked, the baked good or dish is kosher, since there are three doubts here: a) perhaps there were no sheratzim in the flour; b) perhaps they did not leave it and are not forbidden; c) even if there was a sheretz there that left and returned, perhaps during the kneading and baking or cooking it dissolved and lost the status of a beria and was nullified in sixty.
Apparently, the main discussions of the poskim regarding flour concerned the "flour worms" called "milvin" (mealworms), which are larvae of the flour beetle, whose size is between half a centimeter and three centimeters. In recent generations tiny sheratzim of the mite family, called "flour mites," were identified in flour; their color and size are similar to a grain of flour, between 0.3 and 0.6 millimeters, so that an ordinary person is unable to identify them. The flour mite develops in hot and humid areas, at temperatures above 30 degrees. According to the stringent they are forbidden, and in order to sift them out one must sift with a 70-mesh silk sieve, and after the fact with about 60 mesh, or buy flour purified of sheratzim in vacuum packaging, which ensures that tiny sheratzim will not develop in the flour. However, their stringency contradicts tradition, since until about fifty years ago these silk sieves were not available. And even according to halakha one need not be concerned about such tiny sheratzim, as explained in halakha 7. In addition, even with ordinary sheratzim, the reason for checking flour is the concern that they left and returned, but with tiny sheratzim there is almost no concern that they left, since their whole world is the flour; all the more so than what the Baḥ wrote regarding the small worms of his day (84:5). Therefore, it is enough to sift the flour with a 30-mesh sieve, through which tiny sheratzim visible to the ordinary eye do not pass.

sections.body_en:
In the past flour became wormy for two reasons: first, the milling was not complete, and therefore eggs remained in the flour, from which sheratzim hatched; second, flying and crawling sheratzim reached the flour and laid eggs in it, from which the sheratzim hatched. Today, however, following technological improvements and the public's demand for high-quality produce clean of sheratzim, the condition of flour marketed for home consumption in developed countries has greatly improved. To this end, the reliable companies make sure that the flour is milled well, so that most of the eggs are destroyed in the milling, and in order to destroy the remaining ones, they use nitrogen gas or heat the flour. Immediately afterward the flour is packed in sealed bags to protect it. However, when flour packages are left in dirty places, or on the floor, or for a long time on the shelf or in a warehouse, there is a reasonable chance that sheratzim will pierce the packaging and lay eggs in the flour.

Therefore, white flour marketed in sealed packages by reliable companies through responsible chains and stores, and stored at home in a clean place for no more than a few weeks, is presumed clean of sheratzim, and there is no need to sift it, since all the rare cases in which sheratzim are found in it do not reach the level of a "common minority." However, when pouring out the flour, it is advisable to look at it with an ordinary glance, to see that it is indeed clean, as is usual.

But white flour bought wholesale or at the market must be sifted. Likewise, flour of reliable companies must be sifted if it was bought in stores where merchandise remains on the shelf or in the warehouse for a long time, or if it was stored in a dirty place or on the floor. In businesses, too, the flour should be sifted, since they usually buy it wholesale and cheaply, and they generally do not have good conditions for storing it.

Even flour known to be clean, or that has been sifted, if it was left in the open air or in an open package for a full day – and on a hot day even a few hours – may become wormy, and therefore it must be sifted. One who wants to ensure that the flour will not become wormy after opening the package or after sifting should store it in the refrigerator.

One who buys flour from a source about which there is doubt should check it as long as he estimates that a sheretz will frequently be found in it; and if his assessment changes and he thinks that a sheretz will be found in it only rarely, he will no longer need to check flour from that source. A company or store whose flour is considered clean, and in which sheratzim were found several times, has lost its presumption, and from then on one must be careful to sift the flour bought from it. But if this happened because, exceptionally, this flour was stored in a place prone to infestation, it has not lost its presumption (see above, n. 6, on the definitions of a "common minority").

Whole-wheat flour requires sifting, because it is coarsely ground and sometimes eggs remain in it. Some companies market whole-wheat flour in which they destroyed the eggs by means of nitrogen and packed it in vacuum packaging; their flour is presumed clean and does not require checking. Also, some companies market flour that has been kept refrigerated from the time of its milling, and as long as one takes care that it does not go a full day without refrigeration, there is no obligation to check it, because the eggs do not hatch in cold conditions. If the buyer does not know the quality of the whole-wheat flour from the company he buys from, he should check it, and when he estimates that a sheretz will be found in it only rarely, he will no longer need to check it.

Worms found in the flesh of a domestic or wild animal while it is alive, or in the flesh of a bird while it is alive, are forbidden. For if they penetrated from outside, they already became forbidden while they were outside, since they swarmed on the ground. And if they developed in the flesh – just as it is forbidden to eat the meat without slaughter, so it is forbidden to eat worms that developed in it. Even after slaughter the worms remain forbidden, for slaughter permits only the flesh of the domestic animal, wild animal or bird, and not the worms in the flesh.

But there is no prohibition regarding worms that developed in the flesh of a domestic animal, wild animal or bird after its slaughter, for their law is like that of worms that developed in detached fruits, which, as long as they have not left, are not forbidden (above, halakha 3). Likewise is the law of worms that developed in cheese: as long as they have not left it, they are not forbidden. However, whenever there is a feeling of disgust regarding them, it is forbidden to eat them because of the prohibition of bal teshaktzu (above, halakha 2).22

Meat marketed in reliable stores is clean of sheratzim, because strict adherence to the cleanliness and health regulations for preventing the danger of disease and contamination also prevents the development of sheratzim in the meat. However, when preparing the meat in the kitchen and serving it, one must protect it from sheratzim and flies. In large kitchens it is advisable to install screens and traps for flies and mosquitoes, in order to prevent the infestation of the meat and other foods.23

notes_en.en:
So it is explained in Ḥullin 67b, in accordance with the opinion of the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim; and so wrote the Rif, Rashba, Rosh, Ra'ah, Ran and Rema, and this is also the main opinion in SA 84:16. According to them, with fish one is lenient even regarding worms that developed in it while it was alive (as will be explained in the next halakha). These worms develop in meat from eggs that sheratzim laid in the flesh of animals, or from sheretz eggs that the animals swallow, or from larvae or tiny sheratzim invisible to the eye that penetrate the flesh and develop in it. However, the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 2:17) and the Terumah are stringent in two laws: a) regarding worms that developed in the flesh of a domestic or wild animal after slaughter; b) regarding worms that developed in live fish, either because these are worms that began to develop in the water and from there penetrated the flesh of the fish, or because the law of a live fish is like that of attached fruits, where the worms that grow in them are considered as swarming in the water.
The poskim disagreed regarding worms that grew in slaughtered meat, in cheese or in fish, and left them. Some say that even after they have completely left they are permitted, since swarming forbids only with something that grows from the ground (Ra'avya). Some say that while they are in the bowl they are permitted, and when they leave it they are forbidden because of mar'it ayin (how it appears to onlookers) (Rema; Shakh 46). And some say that only while they are on the fish or the cheese are they kosher, but when they leave them, even within the bowl, they become forbidden by Torah law, since they have swarmed on the ground (Levush, Pri Ḥadash, Pri To'ar, Arukh Ha-shulḥan 84:93).

In the summer months there are flies that are able to smell meat from a great distance, reach it, and lay eggs in it from which worms hatch within a few hours. As long as the worms do not leave the meat, according to the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim they do not carry the prohibition of sheratzim, while according to the Rambam and the Terumah they are forbidden. However, according to all opinions they carry the prohibition of bal teshaktzu, because they are repulsive. There is a large fly that lays maggots which immediately burrow into the meat, and it seems that they are forbidden according to all the Rishonim even without having left. Therefore, one should prepare meat, fish and eggs in clean places, and when there is a concern that flies will reach them, one should be careful to cover them with a vessel or plastic wrap immediately after preparing them.

sections.body_en:
Worms that developed in the flesh of a fish, whether alive or dead, as long as they have not left it, are not forbidden. In this the law of fish differs from that of meat: with meat, only worms that developed in it after slaughter are not forbidden (as explained in the previous halakha), whereas with fish, even worms that developed in it while it was alive are not forbidden, since they are subordinate to the flesh of the fish, which is permitted to eat without slaughter.

But worms that penetrated the flesh of the fish from outside are forbidden, since the prohibition already applied to them before they penetrated it. Therefore, worms found in the intestines of a fish, or around the cavities of its mouth and the gills in its head, or adjacent to its skin, are forbidden, since they reached it from the water in which it lives. This phenomenon is common, and therefore it is advisable to buy fish that reliable supervision certifies as clean of worms. When such fish cannot be obtained, or when buying live fish, one should throw away its internal organs, peel off its skin, scrub its outer side and its inner side adjacent to its innards, and clean the area of the mouth and gills well. Those who wish to make it easier for themselves should throw away the head instead of cleaning all the parts adjacent to the openings of its mouth and gills, where the worms are found.

A question arose regarding salmon and other fish such as herring. These fish swallow tiny sheratzim, which had previously swallowed tiny larvae. Inside the intestines of the fish these tiny larvae develop into worms called Anisakis worms, whose length reaches up to ten centimeters and whose color tends toward transparent. As long as the fish is alive they are unable to penetrate from its intestines into its flesh, but after the fish is killed, if it is not frozen immediately, the worms penetrate from its intestines into its flesh. Some say that since the tiny larva began to develop outside the fish, the prohibition already applied to it, and therefore one must supervise that there are no Anisakis worms in salmon and similar fish. And some say that since at the time it was swallowed this larva was tiny (a tenth of a mm), such that an ordinary person, even if he opened the intestines of the small sheretz that swallowed the tiny larva, would not be able to discern it, the prohibition did not apply to this tiny larva. Consequently, the law of Anisakis worms is like that of worms that developed in the flesh of the fish, which, as long as they have not left it, are not forbidden.

As for the halakha, the main view is that of the lenient, since before the larva entered the intestines of the fish it was tiny and not discernible, and it is considered as if it developed in the body of the fish. However, ab initio it is good to be stringent, for in addition to the opinion of the stringent, these worms are large, and consequently their repulsiveness is more noticeable (above, 2); and also, from a health standpoint, they may cause disease. In practice, since it is difficult to check the flesh of the fish for Anisakis worms, as their color is transparent, it is proper to buy fish with kashrut supervision that oversees this.24

notes_en.en: The opinion of the stringent is explained at length by Rav Revaḥ (Tola'at Shani vol. 1, 3:7; vol. 2, sections 3-5). And so wrote Le-horot Natan vol. 9, YD 25, and Shevet Ha-levi 4:83 leaned toward this. On the other hand, many ruled to permit, as cited in Bedikat Ha-mazon Ka-halakha vol. 1, ch. 3, n. 22, in the name of Rav Feinstein, Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, Rav Ben-Tziyon Abba Shaul, and many others.
